summary: Defines SNMP management objects that expose a RADIUS accounting server, which receives usage records. It is informational and was replaced by RFC 4671.

plainLanguage.summary: Gauges on the bookkeeper machine that receives usage records, showing how many arrived and whether it kept up.

subtitle: SNMP management objects for monitoring RADIUS accounting servers

tldr.problem: RADIUS accounting servers process usage records and need to be monitored, but there were no standard management objects defined for them.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2621 defines a MIB module with scalar counters for server-wide statistics (requests, responses, errors) and a client table tracking per-client accounting activity.
tldr.outcome: Administrators can now monitor RADIUS accounting servers using SNMP, observing request rates, error conditions, and per-client metrics. This was replaced by RFC 4671 with an updated MIB.

today: RFC 2621 is Informational and was obsoleted by RFC 4671, which provides an updated RADIUS Accounting Server MIB.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RADIUS accounting servers are machines that collect usage records (called Accounting-Requests) from network access servers and send back Accounting-Responses. Many Internet Service Providers use them to track dial-up sessions for billing.

RFC 2621 defines a set of SNMP objects (a MIB module) that let administrators monitor the health and activity of these servers in real time. The MIB is compliant with SMIv2, the current SNMP management information structure standard.
sections.plainLanguage: RADIUS accounting servers keep records of who used the network. These SNMP objects let you see how the server is doing.

sections.title: The MIB Structure
sections.content:
The RADIUS Accounting Server MIB has two main parts: thirteen scalar objects and a table of clients.

The scalar objects track server-wide statistics: total requests received, invalid requests from unknown addresses, duplicate requests, total responses sent, malformed requests, requests with bad authenticators, packets silently dropped, requests received but not recorded, and requests with unknown types. The MIB also includes the server's implementation identifier, uptime, reset time, and a control object to trigger a server reset.

The client table contains one row for each RADIUS accounting client that shares a secret with the server. Each row shows per-client versions of the key statistics: requests, duplicate requests, responses sent, bad authenticators, malformed requests, dropped packets, and unrecorded requests.
sections.plainLanguage: The MIB is like a dashboard with two parts. The first shows how many requests the whole server got and how many had problems. The second shows those same stats broken down for each client connecting to it.

sections.title: Monitoring with SNMP
sections.content:
An SNMP management station can read the MIB objects to monitor server activity. Each counter is read-only, so SNMP monitors cannot change the statistics, but one object, radiusAccServConfigReset, is read-write. Setting it to 'reset' reinitializes the server's persistent state as if it had just started.

The counters help detect problems: a high count of bad authenticators might indicate misconfiguration or an attack, unrecorded requests suggest the server may be overwhelmed, and silent packet drops may point to resource exhaustion.
sections.plainLanguage: You can look at the numbers to see if the server is healthy. A special control lets you restart it if needed.

sections.title: Security
sections.content:
Some MIB objects expose sensitive information. radiusAccClientAddress reveals the IP address of RADIUS accounting clients, and radiusAccClientID shows their identifiers. An attacker learning these could try to impersonate a legitimate client.

The RFC advises controlling access to these objects, recommending SNMPv3 with user-based security and view-based access control instead of SNMPv1, which offers no built-in security. It also recommends encrypting SNMP messages over the network.
sections.plainLanguage: The list of which clients connected to the server is secret information. You should only let trusted people read it, and send that information encrypted over the network.
